full_name: Two-Phase Randomized Stochastic Gradient Descent (2-RSGD) for Unconstrained Nonconvex Stochastic Optimization
source_reference: Lan, First-order and Stochastic Optimization Methods for Machine Learning, Springer 2020 (Theorem 6.2)

problem.description: Unconstrained nonlinear programming problem; f is differentiable, not necessarily convex, and bounded from below.

assumptions.name: bounded_below
assumptions.math: where f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} is a differentiable (not necessarily convex), bounded from below,

assumptions.name: RSGD_history_measurability
assumptions.math: \text{Note that the search point }x_k\text{ is a function of the history }\xi_{[k-1]}\text{ of the generated random process and hence is random.}

assumptions.name: independent_optimization_runs
assumptions.math: \text{This procedure consists of two phases: an optimization phase used to generate a list of candidate solutions via a few independent runs of the RSGD method and a post-optimization phase in which a solution is selected from this candidate list.}
assumptions.description: The optimization phase loop states that for s=1,...,S, RSGD is called with input x_1, iteration limit N, stepsizes {\gamma_k} in (6.1.21), and probability mass function P_R in (6.1.11), and that \bar{x}_s is the output of this procedure (p. 314, lines 18456-18461). The proof of (6.1.37) then uses the fact that \bar{x}_s, 1 \le s \le S, are independent (p. 316, lines 18555-18557).

assumptions.name: post_optimization_SFO_samples
assumptions.math: \text{where }G(x,\xi_k),\ k=1,\ldots,T,\text{ are the stochastic gradients returned by the SFO.}
assumptions.description: This source sentence identifies the post-optimization samples used in the proof. The PDF later invokes Assumption 13 and Lemma 6.1(a) for these samples, but does not print the specialized filtration or conditional-oracle bridge needed to turn the unconditional oracle statement into Lemma 6.1(a)'s conditional martingale hypothesis.

initialization.math: \text{Input: Initial point }x_1,\text{ number of runs }S,\text{ iteration limit }N,\text{ and sample size }T.

steps.name: RSGD Step 0
steps.math: \text{Let }R\text{ be a random variable with probability mass function }P_R.

steps.name: Optimization phase
steps.math: \text{For }s=1,\ldots,S\text{, call the RSGD method with input }x_1,\text{ iteration limit }N,\text{ stepsizes }\{\gamma_k\}\text{ in (6.1.21) and probability mass function }P_R\text{ in (6.1.11). Let }\bar{x}_s\text{ be the output of this procedure.}

steps.name: Candidate selection
steps.math: \text{Choose a solution }\bar{x}^*\text{ from the candidate list }\{\bar{x}_1,\ldots,\bar{x}_S\}\text{ such that }\|g(\bar{x}^*)\|=\min_{s=1,\ldots,S}\|g(\bar{x}_s)\|.

output.type: selected candidate with smallest empirical gradient norm

main_theorem.statement_math: \text{Under Assumption 13, the following statements hold for the 2-RSGD method applied to problem (6.1.1).}\quad\text{(a) Let }\mathcal{B}_N\text{ be defined in (6.1.22). We have }\operatorname{Prob}\left\{\|\nabla f(\bar{x}^*)\|^2\ge 2\left(4L\mathcal{B}_N+\frac{3\lambda\sigma^2}{T}\right)\right\}\le\frac{S+1}{\lambda}+2^{-S},\quad\forall\lambda>0;\quad\text{(b) Let }\varepsilon>0\text{ and }\Lambda\in(0,1)\text{ be given. If the parameters }(S,N,T)\text{ are set to }S=S(\Lambda):=\left\lceil\log(2/\Lambda)\right\rceil,\;N=N(\varepsilon):=\left\lceil\max\left\{\frac{32L^2D_f^2}{\varepsilon},\left[32L\left(\widetilde{D}+\frac{D_f^2}{\widetilde{D}}\right)\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}\right]^2\right\}\right\rceil,\;T=T(\varepsilon,\Lambda):=\left\lceil\frac{24(S+1)\sigma^2}{\Lambda\varepsilon}\right\rceil,\text{ then the 2-RSGD method can compute an }(\varepsilon,\Lambda)\text{-solution of problem (6.1.1) after taking at most }S(\Lambda)[N(\varepsilon)+T(\varepsilon,\Lambda)]\text{ calls to the stochastic first-order oracle.}
main_theorem.rate: \mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log(1/\Lambda)}{\varepsilon}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{1}{\Lambda}+\frac{\log^2(1/\Lambda)\sigma^2}{\Lambda\varepsilon}\right),\text{ after disregarding constant factors, as in Eq. (6.1.40).}
main_theorem.measure: high-probability bound on the squared gradient norm and SFO complexity for an (epsilon, Lambda)-solution

key_lemmas.name: RSGD_stationarity_bound
key_lemmas.proof_status: blocked_at_source_boundary: Eq. (6.1.18) requires a conditional-oracle/filtration bridge not supplied by Assumption 13 as stated, so Eq. (6.1.19) and all subsequent theorem-bound steps remain source assertions or conditional consequences.
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Suppose that the stepsizes }\{\gamma_k\}\text{ and the probability mass function }P_R(\cdot)\text{ in the RSGD method are chosen such that }\gamma_k<2/L\text{ and }P_R(k):=\operatorname{Prob}\{R=k\}=\frac{2\gamma_k-L\gamma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^N(2\gamma_k-L\gamma_k^2)},\ k=1,\ldots,N.\text{ Then, under Assumption 13, (a) for any }N\ge 1,\text{ we have }\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(x_R)\|^2]\le\frac{D_f^2+\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^N(2\gamma_k-L\gamma_k^2)},\text{ where the expectation is taken with respect to }R\text{ and }\xi_{[N]}:=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N),\ D_f:=\left[\frac{2(f(x_1)-f^*)}{L}\right]^{1/2},\text{ and }f^*\text{ denotes the optimal value of problem (6.1.1).}

key_lemmas.name: Constant_stepsize_bound
key_lemmas.proof_status: conditional_on_RSGD_stationarity_bound: the source's constant-stepsize algebra is recorded, but the expectation-bound conclusion is not discharged because Theorem 6.1(a) is blocked at Eqs. (6.1.18)-(6.1.19).
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Suppose that the stepsizes }\{\gamma_k\}\text{ are set to }\gamma_k=\min\left\{\frac{1}{L},\frac{\widetilde{D}}{\sigma\sqrt{N}}\right\},\ k=1,\ldots,N,\text{ for some }\widetilde{D}>0.\text{ Also assume that the probability mass function }P_R(\cdot)\text{ is set to (6.1.11). Then, under Assumption 13, we have }\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(x_R)\|^2]\le\mathcal{B}_N:=\frac{LD_f^2}{N}+\left(\widetilde{D}+\frac{D_f^2}{\widetilde{D}}\right)\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}},\text{ where }D_f\text{ is defined in (6.1.13)}.

key_lemmas.name: Martingale_second_moment_bound
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that we are given a polish space with Borel probability measure }\mu\text{ and a sequence of }\mathcal{F}_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_1\subseteq\mathcal{F}_2\subseteq\cdots\text{ of }\sigma\text{-sub-algebras of Borel }\sigma\text{-algebra of }\Omega.\text{ Let }\zeta_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ i=1,\ldots,\infty,\text{ be a martingale-difference sequence of Borel functions on }\Omega\text{ such that }\zeta_i\text{ is }\mathcal{F}_i\text{ measurable and }\mathbb{E}[\zeta_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0,\text{ where }\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_i]\text{ denotes conditional expectation with respect to }\mathcal{F}_i\text{ and }\mathbb{E}\equiv\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_0]\text{ is expectation with respect to }\mu.\text{ (a) If }\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta_i\|^2]\le\sigma_i^2\text{ for any }i\ge 1,\text{ then }\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N\zeta_i\right\|^2\right]\le\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i^2.\text{ As a consequence, }\forall N\ge 1,\lambda\ge 0:\ \operatorname{Prob}\left\{\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N\zeta_i\right\|^2\ge\lambda\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i^2\right\}\le\frac{1}{\lambda}.
key_lemmas.role: Controls each post-optimization empirical-gradient error and the union-bound term in Theorem 6.2.

key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Assume that we are given a polish space with Borel probability measure }\mu\text{ and a sequence of }\mathcal{F}_0=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_1\subseteq\mathcal{F}_2\subseteq\cdots\text{ of }\sigma\text{-sub-algebras of Borel }\sigma\text{-algebra of }\Omega.\text{ Let }\zeta_i\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ i=1,\ldots,\infty,\text{ be a martingale-difference sequence of Borel functions on }\Omega\text{ such that }\zeta_i\text{ is }\mathcal{F}_i\text{ measurable and }\mathbb{E}[\zeta_i\mid\mathcal{F}_{i-1}]=0,\text{ where }\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_i]\text{ denotes the conditional expectation with respect to }\mathcal{F}_i\text{ and }\mathbb{E}\equiv\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_0]\text{ is expectation with respect to }\mu.\text{ (a) If }\mathbb{E}[\|\zeta_i\|^2]\le\sigma_i^2\text{ for any }i\ge 1,\text{ then }\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N\zeta_i\right\|^2\right]\le\sum_{i=1}^N\sigma_i^2.
